name: Standing Dumbbell Biceps Curl
variant: Standing bilateral or alternating supinated dumbbell curl, performed without bench, preacher-pad, cable, or machine support.
description: Stand tall with dumbbells at the sides, keep the elbows near the ribs and the wrists controlled, curl by flexing the elbows while turning or keeping the palms supinated, then lower under control until the elbows are long without swinging the torso.

hypertrophy.rationale: A direct elbow-flexor hypertrophy accessory with good biceps exposure, but less constant resistance than cable and less long-length bias than incline variants.

strength.rationale: Builds local elbow-flexion strength, but the loading ceiling and systemic carryover are much lower than compound pulling movements.

joint_resilience.rationale: Provides controlled elbow and wrist loading, but it is not a broad joint-capacity exercise.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Transfer is narrow because the movement is a single-joint arm accessory with little whole-body coordination demand.

control.rationale: Requires wrist position, elbow path, and anti-swing discipline, but little balance or bracing.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Delivers focused arm stimulus with low systemic fatigue when performed strictly.

setup.rationale: Requires only matching dumbbells and floor space.

ease.rationale: Simple to learn and adjust, with the main technical issue being torso swing and elbow drift.

progression.rationale: Reps and load are easy to track, but dumbbell jumps can be coarse at lighter loads.

support.rationale: No external support is provided; the user controls posture, shoulders, elbows, and wrists.

primary.name: Biceps brachii
primary.evidenceShort: Standing dumbbell curl EMG directly measured biceps brachii activity.
primary.evidence: The standing dumbbell curl condition directly measured biceps brachii activity, and broader curl-variant EMG evidence supports high biceps involvement in supinated curl patterns.

secondary.name: Brachialis
secondary.evidenceShort: Deep elbow flexor contribution is expected during loaded elbow flexion.
secondary.evidence: Brachialis is included from elbow-flexion anatomy and curl handgrip mechanics. Surface EMG sources often cannot isolate it cleanly because it is deep, so it is classified as secondary rather than primary for this supinated dumbbell variant.

secondary.name: Brachioradialis
secondary.evidenceShort: Curl EMG studies directly measure brachioradialis contribution.
secondary.evidence: Curl variant and handgrip studies directly measured brachioradialis activity during dumbbell, bar, and grip-position curl conditions. It is secondary because a supinated dumbbell biceps curl is primarily programmed for biceps brachii.

support.name: Wrist flexors
support.evidenceShort: Grip and wrist posture require forearm support.
support.evidence: Forearm EMG sources show wrist flexor activity during wrist and grip-related tasks. They are listed as support because the dumbbell must be held with a stable wrist, not because this is a wrist-flexion exercise.

evidence.verdict: Standing dumbbell biceps curl: biceps brachii primary; brachialis and brachioradialis secondary; wrist flexors support.
evidence.clinicalShort: Surface EMG estimates acute excitation and does not directly prove hypertrophy, strength transfer, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Supination timing, dumbbell path, elbow drift, torso swing, load, tempo, and alternating versus bilateral execution can shift emphasis.
evidence.summary: The standing dumbbell biceps curl is classified as a simple free-weight elbow-flexion accessory. Direct dumbbell-curl EMG supports biceps brachii as the main target, while broader curl handgrip evidence supports brachioradialis involvement. Brachialis is included conservatively as a secondary deep elbow flexor, and wrist flexors are shown only as grip and wrist-position support.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: This movement is best used as a low-friction arm hypertrophy accessory. It should remain separate from incline, preacher, cable, hammer, reverse, and machine curl variants because shoulder position, resistance curve, grip, and external support change the stimulus.
evidence.limitations: The standing dumbbell curl is easy to alter unintentionally through shoulder flexion, upper-arm drift, supination timing, and torso swing. Brachialis evidence is partly anatomical because the main surface EMG sources do not isolate it directly.

studies.finding: Compared biceps brachii EMG across incline dumbbell curl, standing dumbbell curl, and preacher curl conditions.
studies.citation: Oliveira LF, Matta TT, Alves DS, Garcia MAC, Vieira TMM. Effect of the shoulder position on the biceps brachii EMG in different dumbbell curls. Journal of Sports Science and Medicine. 2009;8(1):24-29.
studies.relevance: Direct standing dumbbell curl evidence for biceps brachii activity and shoulder-position variant boundaries.

studies.finding: Straight barbell, EZ-bar, and dumbbell curls produced different biceps brachii and brachioradialis EMG patterns across repetition phases.
studies.citation: Marcolin G, Panizzolo FA, Petrone N, Moro T, Grigoletto D, Piccolo D, Paoli A. Differences in electromyographic activity of biceps brachii and brachioradialis while performing three variants of curl. PeerJ. 2018;6:e5165. doi:10.7717/peerj.5165.
studies.relevance: Direct dumbbell and bar curl evidence for biceps brachii and brachioradialis recruitment.

studies.finding: Supinated, pronated, and neutral cable curl handgrips changed biceps brachii, brachioradialis, and anterior deltoid excitation in competitive bodybuilders.
studies.citation: Coratella G, Tornatore G, Longo S, Toninelli N, Padovan R, Esposito F, Ce E. Biceps Brachii and Brachioradialis Excitation in Biceps Curl Exercise: Different Handgrips, Different Synergy. Sports. 2023;11(3):64. doi:10.3390/sports11030064.
studies.relevance: Handgrip-specific curl evidence for biceps brachii, brachioradialis, and grip-position boundaries.

studies.type: Forearm rotation and wrist muscle EMG
studies.shortCitation: Ikeda et al., J Orthop Surg Res, 2025
studies.finding: Wrist flexor and extensor activity changed with forearm rotation during controlled wrist torque tasks.
studies.citation: Ikeda K, Kaneoka K, Matsunaga N, Ikumi A, Yamazaki M, Yoshii Y. Effects of forearm rotation on wrist flexor and extensor muscle activities. Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery and Research. 2025;20(1):53. doi:10.1186/s13018-024-05363-x.
studies.relevance: Forearm and wrist-position evidence for grip and wrist support.

studies.type: Forearm EMG during wrist and finger movements
studies.finding: Multi-channel EMG quantified forearm muscle activity during wrist and finger movement tasks.
studies.citation: Gazzoni M, Celadon N, Mastrapasqua D, Paleari M, Margaria V, Ariano P. Quantifying forearm muscle activity during wrist and finger movements by means of multi-channel electromyography. PLoS ONE. 2014;9(10):e109943. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0109943.
studies.relevance: Broader forearm EMG context for gripping and wrist-position stabilization.
